Accuracy is reported for one fixed seed despite stochastic single-sample optimization. There are no confidence intervals, repeated-seed results, or paired significance tests. No theoretical justification or empirical calibration establishes the claimed relationship, undermining the paper's central mechanism and interpretation.

The paper incorrectly states that the reward is non-differentiable with respect to the input embeddings. Transformer logits are differentiable with respect to those embeddings, and top-k selection is differentiable almost everywhere once the selected indices are fixed. The paper omits the essential direct-gradient baseline. Its alternative is a one-sample, baseline-free score-function estimator in a very high-dimensional space, which should have extreme variance; no gradient-quality analysis, multiple-seed evaluation, or variance results are provided.

The evaluation protocol risks test-set overfitting. Six hyperparameters are selected separately for nearly every model-dataset pair. For MATH-500 and AIME, which lack training splits, the authors use a GSM8K proxy and then make unspecified 'minimal adjustments,' apparently using the evaluation tasks themselves. Search spaces, trial counts, and selection criteria are not reported. The fixed configuration only covers one model and may itself have been chosen post hoc.

The headline AIME evidence is statistically inadequate. Each AIME set has only 30 questions, so reported changes occur in 3.33-point increments and often represent only one or two additional correct answers. The stochastic method is run with one fixed seed, without confidence intervals, paired tests, or repeated runs. Equal-weight averaging across datasets further gives each 30-item AIME set the same influence as much larger benchmarks.

The main robustness claim is confounded by output truncation. Qwen-3-14B's zero-shot AIME average rises from 10% at 4,096 output tokens to 75% at 64,000 tokens; LTPO's remaining advantage is only three answers across 60 questions. Truncation rates and length-controlled comparisons are absent, so apparent reasoning gains may partly reflect shorter generations rather than better reasoning.

Baseline coverage and fairness are insufficient. Missing controls include random latent perturbation/search, direct gradient optimization, alternative uncertainty objectives, and compute-matched decoding or best-of-N methods. SoftCoT is evaluated out of domain using a GSM8K-trained projection, LatentSeek is omitted for two models, and training-based comparisons are not controlled for data or compute. Latency is reported without a fixed disclosed hardware/software setting, FLOPs, memory, or complete token statistics, so it does not establish lower computational cost.

The method is underspecified and internally inconsistent: the formal algorithm never defines the later 'best reward' selection or whether the sampled action or updated mean is retained; exact checkpoint revisions, chat-template settings, seed, parsing code, and non-mathematical-task hyperparameters are absent; no implementation is released. LatentSeek Prompt-1 GSM8K accuracy also changes unexplained from 53.15 in Table 1 to 49.89 in Table 7.

The appendix's theoretical claims do not repair the method. Theorem B.1's iff statement follows only from a first-order infinitesimal approximation, while Theorem B.2 assumes attraction and convergence that do not follow for the stated stochastic, changing-variance algorithm.

Novelty is limited relative to LatentSeek, which already performs instance-level test-time policy-gradient optimization in latent space. The main change is the problematic reward and avoidance of decoding. Moreover, no evidence shows that the optimized vectors encode intermediate reasoning rather than functioning as instance-specific soft prompts that alter confidence, output style, or response length.

The empirical scope is reasonably broad: four models from two families, five mathematical benchmarks, two non-mathematical tasks, and comparisons with CoT, an unoptimized-token control, SoftCoT, and LatentSeek.

The manuscript is generally organized and includes hyperparameter tables, prompt examples, latency and output-length measurements, a fixed-configuration experiment, and an explicit discussion of confidence-correctness divergence.
weaknesses: The central reward is not established as a confidence measure. Equation 4 maximizes the negative mean log-probability of the top-k tokens; for k=1 this strictly rewards a lower maximum probability, while for k>1 it is not monotone in entropy, top-k mass, or ordinary predictive confidence. It can favor pathological diffuse or highly imbalanced distributions. Consequently, the interpretation underlying the method and conclusions is unsupported.

The claim that this reward is non-differentiable with respect to the latent vectors is incorrect: log-softmax and selected top-k values are differentiable almost everywhere, and gradients can be propagated directly to input embeddings while model weights remain frozen. The paper neither evaluates this simpler baseline nor supplies another reason for using high-variance REINFORCE.

The gradient estimator uses one perturbation and an uncentered positive reward in a very high-dimensional space, without a baseline, antithetic sampling, or variance analysis. Constant reward offsets therefore inject substantial noise. There are no random-perturbation, constant-reward, random-search, or compute-matched ablations demonstrating that the proposed update—not stochastic soft-prompt perturbation—causes the gains.

The evaluation uses a single fixed seed and reports no uncertainty or paired significance tests. Each AIME set contains only 30 questions, so many highlighted improvements amount to one or two additional correct answers; the 64k-token result is likewise a one- or two-question difference. Equal-weight averaging across datasets of radically different sizes further magnifies these noisy AIME results.

The main results use six separately selected hyperparameters for nearly every model-dataset pair. For MATH and AIME, which lack training splits, the authors report starting from GSM8K and then making unspecified 'minimal adjustments'; this leaves open direct test-set tuning. Search spaces, trial counts, and selection rules are absent, while the fixed-configuration check covers only one model.

Several comparisons are incomplete or confounded. LatentSeek is omitted for two models; no compute-matched self-consistency or best-of-N baseline is included; and the latency comparison omits the exact-prompt CoT-Unk control even though LTPO's prompt explicitly encourages concise output. The hardware is only identified as one of two substantially different GPUs. LatentSeek's LLaMA GSM8K score also changes unexplained from 53.15 in Table 1 to 49.89 in Table 7.

The paper does not show that the optimized embeddings represent latent reasoning rather than ordinary soft-prompt steering. It provides no quantitative relationship between reward and correctness, no comparison among reasonable confidence objectives, and no analysis of what information the vectors encode. The appendix's 'theorems' are essentially first-order tautologies, overstate an approximate condition as an if-and-only-if result, and do not describe the stochastic algorithm actually used.

Reproducibility remains insufficient: there is no LTPO code link, and important details such as the exact seed, model revisions, precision, parser, chat templates, and hyperparameter-search protocol are missing. Claims such as 'parameter-free,' 'no additional data,' and superiority across all benchmarks are also misleading given the optimized latent parameters, validation-based tuning, and numerous individual benchmark losses.

Because the reward semantics and stated need for policy gradients are technically unsound, while the stochastic and potentially test-tuned evaluation cannot validate the claimed mechanism, the paper has fundamental problems rather than merely missing polish or secondary ablations.
